This research investigates the capabilities of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) in object categorization without the aid of a specific output layer. To address this challenge, the authors introduce a self-supervised learning strategy where the model's objective is to learn a representation that maximizes the mutual information between object categories and the temporal trajectory of its hidden states. Crucially, the study examines the influence of auxiliary tasks on the resulting representation by analyzing both a baseline method and two specific tasks: the first predicts object categories from hidden states immediately, the second performs this prediction after only a few RNN steps. The experiments, which utilize ImageNet as the data source, confirm the sub-network trained with ground truth assistance significantly enhances object categorization accuracy compared to one trained without it. The results indicate that the number of RNN steps required to make an accurate prediction serves as a meaningful feature for the final object representation.

This study investigates the skin effect within non-Hermitian systems that exhibit non-diagonal interactions, specifically focusing on the extended, non-diagonal-coupled, and non-Hermitian-coupled (ENDH) lattice. We find that these correlations modify the conventional bulk-boundary and skin-effect boundary conditions by introducing additional non-diagonal contributions to the corresponding exponents of the theory, yet they do not fundamentally negate the presence of a visible-surface effect. Specifically, in NH chains with non-Hermitian-coupled (NHC) correlations and other related structures, the magnitude of the skin-effect exponent is non-trivially altered, though it is not negated. Notably, in a non-Hermitian-coupled (NCS) system with a particular type of non-Hermitian-coupled (NCCS) correlation and other related structures, the magnitude of the skin-effect exponent is non-trivial, but it is not negated. Therefore, these correlations do non-trivially alter the magnitude of the skin-effect visible-surface effect in non-Hermitian-coupled (NCS) and other related structures.

This paper addresses the generation of quaternary Golay complementary array pairs through a construction method that adds a new dimension. This work presents an updated global analysis of the LHC's vector boson fusion (VBF) and associated production (AP) of the Higgs boson, focusing on anomalous Higgs boson vector boson couplings utilizing latest data from both LHC experiments through a model-independent approach. While previous studies have constrained these couplings based on LHC 2015–2018 findings with limited CERN-MCNULEO collaboration input, this new analysis incorporates a significant contribution from CMS and muon-less electron-neutrino decay channel data. Despite the AP channel showing weaker sensitivity compared to VBF, the integration of AP data enhances the overall sensitivity in both the EEWB and VBF modes. As a result, our findings indicate that these coupling anomalies are tightly restricted to well-inside their standard model predictions.

Recent advancements in unsupervised change detection have proven to be very promising, especially given the difficulty of gathering paired image changes necessary for other approaches. Although requiring no labeled data for training makes this direction theoretically attractive, a significant challenge remains in accurately calibrating these models against a wide variety of scene transitions. We address this by introducing a straightforward yet efficient strategy that simultaneously performs self-calibration for the self-supervised model and learns an auxiliary segmentation model with segmentation tasks. We term this method "segCalib," which effectively guides the self-supervised component's self-calibration through the segCalib model. This approach allows us to achieve superior performance on multiple benchmarks compared to other unsupervised techniques, marking the first successful deployment of such models with a high-accuracy supervised changer detector. We also see that this approach yields a beneficial co-adaptive relationship between models and provides a robust foundation for further research into self-supervised change detection.

To date, there is no clear consensus on whether climate change policy is sufficiently informed by empirical understanding of general science, as well as on the specific attention climate change receives within that broader science landscape. Additionally, evidence regarding how much that policy itself tracks with the evolving field of climate economics is also lacking. To address these knowledge gaps, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of nearly 500 policy documents released between 2013 and 2019 via a database search. We examined the frequency of references to social science and natural science fields, as well as the evolution of policy focus over time. We introduce TuRaN, the world's first Time-Reversible, Multi-Channel, Throughput-Aware, and Energy-Optimized True Random Number Generator (TRNG) that utilizes on-chip analog circuit noise. By integrating a 4-tap, linear feedback shift register as a lightweight randomness amplification layer using only basic XOR operations, the system effectively enhances randomness. This architecture empowers the generation of a parallel random stream, offering the combined advantage of minimal power usage and maximal data-output speed. Our prototype confirms that a single implementation can simultaneously deliver 128 Mbps of true random data while consuming merely 0.73 microjoules per byte, making it the most efficient and high-throughput TRNG to date. These capabilities make TuRaN ideal for applications demanding both massive parallelism and efficient stochastic computing.

The integration of resistive switches into resistive memory arrays poses challenges for fault tolerance, which can be mitigated by implementing single-electron (SE) resistive switches. Defined by a storage node coupled through a single capacitor to two electrodes, these devices feature a tunneling oxide thin enough to enable single-electron charging while maintaining an ON/OFF current ratio on the order of 10^12, vastly exceeding the ~10^3 ratio typical of transition-metal-oxide (TMO) resistive memory. Although individual resistive memory cells generally exhibit lower ratios (~10^5), array feasibility remains possible with such memory. This paper introduces a theoretical single-electron circuit model that numerically explores the dynamic behavior of resistive memory arrays incorporating single-electron switches using spiking input patterns. Results suggest that such arrays achieve fault tolerance through significantly improved spike detection and recovery capabilities when using this design.

This paper examines maximum likelihood and method-of-moments estimation for parameters in causal models of no-one-way-causes (NOCs), which are defined by marginal independence conditions rather than typical chirp sum rules. Our analysis focuses on consistent estimators within solvable NOCs that allow for closed-form formulas; for many such structures, these maximum likelihood estimators also possess consistency properties. This work extends previous work on estimable functions in acyclic and cyclic independence models (e.g., those described in this arXiv:1508.0040) to more complex configurations.

We demonstrate how to identify estimable functions in NOCs using directed paths and provide simple conditions ensuring that functions remain within the set of estimable expressions for all sample sizes. These conditions help verify whether an estimator is consistent for specific no-one-causation models. Our work also includes a discussion on maximizing the likelihood function for these structures using a local search algorithm.

Finally, we extend existing concepts from simpler independence models to more complex scenarios, showing the application of these methods through specific examples.

The paper introduces a new framework for investigating the long-term socioeconomic trajectory of opportunities across generations within a society, aiming to analyze their distribution fairness. The authors define a new metric, the Opportunity Gini Coefficient, which extends the traditional Gini coefficient into the intergenerational domain; this coefficient ranges from 0 to 1, where lower values signify a more equitable society. With this coefficient, one can evaluate critical issues such as the fairness of job assignments and educational access, and also forecast future opportunity gaps. Specifically, it enables the projection of current student debt levels' impact on the socioeconomic status of future cohorts.

This study derives a relationship describing the sign change observed when the coordinates of $N$ identical particles are permuted. While Levenson and Peshkin previously established that the wavefunctions of identical particles exhibit a specific phase factor—$(-1)^{2s}$ in real space, where $2s$ represents the spin of a single particle—we provide a more comprehensive derivation using the Dirac notation of quantum states. Our fundamental argument rests on a previously unproven connection between spatial coordinates and internal state spaces. Specifically, we construct a mapping between these distinct domains by employing quantum-chiral-hyper-nuclei—nuclei possessing spatially disconnected, topologically twisted, and chiral components—that exhibit defined spin and symmetry properties.

Cryptocurrency transactions utilize traditional RingCT privacy methods, which can lead to substantial verification overhead due to large signatures caused by many possible anonymous inputs. This complicates transaction verification, hindering scalability and transaction confirmation speeds. Our solution, dubbed "Delegated RingCT," enhances efficiency by enabling a prover to replace the massive anonymous input selection with a smaller, verified subset, thus allowing the verifier to confirm chain validity faster. Verifying a transaction with this method now only requires checking a limited number of possible anonymous inputs. Our implementation achieves up to an 8-fold speedup over the best existing protocols. Additionally, our system introduces "Aggregated RingCT" for the further optimization of verification processes.

This paper explores linear systems solving as a framework for analyzing computational complexity across different algorithmic approximations. Specifically, we demonstrate that reductions between `gggggggg`-approximate solvers (or even mixing-time-approximations of the corresponding Markov chains) for the same type of linear systems can almost always be realized using constant-depth threshold circuits with depth of just two. Furthermore, our findings significantly simplify existing linear algebraic arguments by showing how reductions involving different solver types can be nearly universally reduced to linear compositions of linear functions. This allows standard complexity-theoretic properties, such as closure under substitutions, to be established with straightforward, almost trivial proofs.

Concurrent deep learning methods have recently been applied to modeling and analyzing systems in solid mechanics, yet almost all existing approaches assume training on a single, static dataset without adapting to new data streams. To address scenarios where systems evolve over time, we introduce a method capable of continuing training on fresh data sequences within a mechanical context, specifically focusing on plasticity. For a given material exhibiting history-dependent behavior, this technique learns an encoding of that history via a neural network while performing analysis, rather than being completely retrained from scratch with each new sequence. Instead, it incorporates the new sequences through further training while being provided with additional input-encoding pairs. This research presents a comprehensive neural network architecture for such sequences, featuring a sequential element to handle the history dependence and a deep, multi-layer sub-component to capture the underlying physical laws. We evaluate the method using a well-documented experimental plasticity dataset, comparing our results against sequential model averaging, the VAE, and models reset with the very first dataset. The findings reveal that continuous learning outperforms all baseline strategies in both accuracy and efficiency while also reducing both computational time and storage requirements associated with brute-force strategies.

In vacuum and weak-decoy quantum key distribution (QKD) protocols, an undetected adversary can execute an elegant attack by decoying with genuine qubits while simultaneously dropping them afterward. Existing generative approaches for generating discrete speech segments face dual challenges: ensuring speech intelligibility while preventing the model from settling into non-dynamic clustering patterns. To prevent this, we introduce a novel two-stage framework. Firstly, we fathom discrete speech synthesis by analyzing current autoencoder methods and identifying the necessity of transient states alongside dynamic clustering to maintain speech quality during generation. Secondly, we establish a variational objective that explicitly penalizes these transient states to foster dynamic clustering. Furthermore, we propose a two-phase training strategy to prevent the collapse of generated clusters during training. Finally, we validate our approach through extensive experiments, demonstrating that this method surpasses all current state-of-the-art systems regarding speech quality.

This study introduces a multi-stage optimization framework dedicated to online motion planning for multi-limbed robots. The primary objective of this system is to enhance computational efficiency during the planning of motion that satisfies both kinematic and dynamic constraints. The architecture consists of a initial phase involving sequential, constraint-based feasibility checks and a secondary phase that performs a multi-objective optimization to refine the trajectory. Specifically, the first phase filters out infeasible motions by isolating violations related to kinematics and dynamics, while the second stage simultaneously optimizes for trajectory smoothness and the specific dysfunctions identified in the initial phase. We also present a feasibility check based on sequential projection that effectively identifies dynamic violations. This projection method converts a time-coupled optimization feasibility test into a series of simpler, time-decoupled checks. Furthermore, by integrating this framework with a randomized motion exploration strategy, the proposed approach achieves a significant reduction in computational time. Simulation results confirm that this multi-stage system markedly decreases computation time compared to standard planning methods.

The velocity gauge within tight-binding models presents significant limitations, specifically an inability to capture the Landau level fan and divergent total magnetization, rendering it ineffective for characterizing electromagnetic responses away from integer filling factors. These deficiencies are resolved by introducing a modified form of the vector potential that retains the local lattice structure and maintains a finite total magnetization across all filling levels. Despite this improvement, the modified velocity gauge remains susceptible to numerical inaccurations characterized by oscillations as a function of the system's linear dimensions. To ensure precision, all calculations derived from this gauge must be performed on large systems. The modified framework was applied to compute the magnetization and optical conductivity for a square tight-binding lattice, revealing quantitative agreement with results obtained using the Landau gauge and confirming that the resulting optical conductivity exhibits a universal scaling behavior as function of the filling factor.

This research introduces a graph-theoretic approach for robust 3D monocular pose and shape estimation from single images of objects with known 3D definitions. The method relies on solving sets of polynomial equations derived by matching 3D-2D feature origins to detect the first 3D-2D line supports. A solution is then refined through the use of 3D-2L quadratic lines derived from matching 3D-2L quadratic curves. Using multiple 3D-2L quadratic matches allows for the estimation of a polynomial that can with stand a high proportion of outliers (up to 80%). The method is validated on real-world monocular video streams, where it achieves an average error rate of less than 5 \% for 3D-2L quadratic matches. This paper examines the confidence region for the Cauchy distribution parameter $\theta$ on the complex plane. Although the Cauchy distribution is a standard choice for modeling datasets comprising real and imaginary parts, its high sample variance often results in low model efficiency. We establish that the distribution's parameter $\theta$, representing the location, corresponds directly to the center of the confounding region when expressed as a point in the complex plane; specifically, this region takes the shape of a $\theta^*$ shape. This shape, defined by our location parameter, allows for improved estimation. We provide a detailed study on optimizing this shape to achieve high sample efficiency. Simulations and real-world analyses confirm that this approach outperforms both full Cauchy models and strategies using only the real or imaginary components separately. We define this new method as the $\theta^*$ estimator.

Borrowing information across subgroups remains a challenging topic in clinical trials; while commensurate subgroups appear identical, they often differ slightly in magnitude regarding treatment effects. This study examines statistical methods for deciding whether to share data between such groups. This decision hinges on estimating the treatment interaction term and its associated uncertainty. This work derives closed-form formulas for the approximate minimum sample size needed to achieve a pre-specified level of precision for this estimate. The sample size is calculated by evaluating the power of a hypothesis test regarding the correlation between treatment effects in subgroups under the null hypothesis that treatment strategies are equivalent (i.e., no interaction). This approach validates and extends the Farcomen and Zelenyuk (2020) proposal, which suggests using predictive distributions under the assumption of treatment commensurability as a proxy for the joint distribution of treatment effects in the absence interaction. The proposed closed-form equations are demonstrated through both a simulation study and an analysis of bowel cancer trial regarding the S-1 vs capecitabine. This final analysis shows that, in this specific trial context, the level of uncertainty regarding the need to adjust the S-1 dose was low, indicating a high likelihood that the dose does not vary by body size.

This paper introduces an enhanced observer for tracking nominal motion under dynamic constraints that depend on the current position, addressing how these varying dynamics adversely affect real-world tracking. The difficulty of the non-linear inequality constraints is eliminated through a transformation of the problem into zero-level set equations, which an auxiliary controller forces the system to satisfy with high precision. The finite-time convergence of both the state estimator and the controller is proven, with simulation results effectively demonstrating its performance and validity.

Extensive experiments on the standard benchmark datasets 6DOF and benchmark4 demonstrate that this approach yields significantly strong results. This study investigates the conditions under which ground noise becomes audible during impact events. While continuous ground noise is often invisible to the air, it can be detected in the air when the ground's vibrational strength is sufficient to generate strong source effects. The source is determined by interface conditions between the ground and the air; these conditions vary based on how the ground surface is covered and its structural type. Consequently, ground noise might be heard not just during direct ground contact, but also during direct air contact in specific scenarios. We present an analytical derivation of these conditions across various surface types—ranging from unbounded to semi-bounded and sealed configurations—and different models, including acoustic, elastic, and acoustic-elastic cases—using both the strain and the vertical velocity at the interface as primary variables. The findings indicate that ground noise is typically inaudible in the air except when impacts occur with a rigid object, such as a rigid sphere, against these surfaces. Additionally, specific situations allow for the simultaneous perception of the same ground noise through the air, the ground, or both media.

This setup generalizes the standard bipartite nonlocality test, and our results are applicable to both quantum and classical protocols. We demonstrate that, for any input probability distribution and arbitrary strategy by the agents, there exist specific correlation patterns that consistently outperform random strategies by the other $N-1$ participants. These findings, which might initially appear to restrict the scope of these phenomena, actually broaden the interest in them. This is because the non-random, optimized correlations can still exhibit nonlocal behavior or violate non-trivial contextuality conditions. Consequently, our work suggests that these effects may emerge in more extensive protocols that engage $N$ agents rather than remaining confined to bipartite interactions.

This paper addresses the existence of isolated points within the space of actions on a topological discrete group $\Gamma$, where those actions are equipped with the topology of pointwise convergence. Formal verification techniques like model checking have become an essential component in the development of automotive driving systems. These methods examine system models to guarantee that particular specifications are met. This paper presents a unified framework for executing both stochastic model checking and dynamic programing on a class of hybrid automata known as one-dimensional switchable continuous automata. Associated with this framework are two model-checking algorithms that are proven correct. The paper additionally details the adaptation of various data structures for implementing stochastic model checking. Finally, the practical application of this approach is demonstrated through the model-checking analysis of a cooperative adaptive cruise control system.

The Koopman operator framework offers a promising approach to analyzing nonlinear dynamical systems by linearizing their behavior, yet this relies on constructing eigen-decompositions that remain challenging with high-dimensional data. This study introduces a new method to perform low-rank approximations of the Koopman operator applicable to systems defined on manifolds. Based on this approximation, several algorithms are developed to estimate eigenpairs efficiently. Demonstrating efficacy in the Koopman-based reconstruction of system dynamics and analysis of geometric observables, this research presents the results on synthetic and real-world applications.

Historically, infinite magnitude has served as a catalyst for theoretical advancements across numerous academic fields. Throughout its evolution, definitions of "infinity" have varied among scholars. Specifically, the 17th century saw two distinct conceptions coexist: "bounded infinity" and "unbounded infinity." While the contemporary view typically equates the latter solely with "unlimited," historical analysis reveals that the distinction between these concepts was more nuanced. This response clarifies and expands upon the inherent meanings of bounded and unbounded infinity as envisioned by Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz. Furthermore, we examine the critical distinction between an infinite process (an *actus infinitus*) and the notion of actual infinity (an *entitas infinita*), a topic of significant debate within medieval scholasticism. By tracing the philosophical foundations of these ideas within the works of Leibniz and examining their mathematical implications, we aim to provide a comprehensive understanding of their philosophical importance.

We conduct a simulation study to evaluate the recovery of CMB lensing from simulated foreground-subtracted data sets that include realistic effects like foreground modeling uncertainties and unmodeled residuals. Our simulations show that foreground removal significantly biases parameter recovery if flaws occur in the subtraction process; specifically, imperfect subtraction leads to power spectrum mismatches between the model and data that mimic foreground shapes in lensing templates, causing the estimator to reject foreground components and flatten the spectrum at multipoles $l \gtrsim 500$. Additionally, we create and solve a system of equations to translate mismatches in the lensing power spectrum into estimates of foreground model errors in the map domain. This analysis reveals that foreground errors translate to bias in CMB lensing amplitude $A_{\rm L}$ approximately linearly with a slope of $\sim 1$ for large amplitudes, though the relationship becomes non-linear for smaller amplitudes. To address this, we formulate a non-linear correction formula designed to improve the accuracy of $A_{\rm L}$ estimates in such scenarios.

Recent recommender system research has highlighted the challenge of document modeling as a means to mitigate issues arising from sparse user interaction data. By representing documents through specific user behavior sequences, these methods capture distinct characteristics that standard item factor models often overlook, thereby potentially raising prediction accuracy. However, because documents and users share the same embedding space, capturing both entities simultaneously remains difficult, particularly when documents have limited associated tags. This study introduces PUDVAE (Sparse Paper Recommendation with PUDVAE), a novel joint learning framework that simultaneously models documents and users via probabilistic latent factor analysis. PUDVAE effectively balances these two complex modeling tasks and, for the first time, integrates user behavior tags into the documents' embedding space. Experiments on two real-world datasets confirm that this approach substantially boosts recommendation performance.

Conditionally, we prove that the semicircle law persists even when the standard assumption of independent identically distributed (i.i.d.) entries is replaced by conditional independence and conditional identically distributed (conditional I.I.D) structures. Furthermore, we derive explicit I.I.D. samples for the entries of conditionally I.I.D. matrices. These I.I.D. samples are determined by a total I.I.D. set of the matrix entries and the condition itself. This I.I.D. property holds true regardless of whether the conditional independence refers to any fixed event or a random variable. This methodology enables the I.I.D. approximation of joint eigenvalue distributions in various applications. As an illustration, we demonstrate how to jointly approximate the eigenvalues of the product derived from conditionally I.I.D. matrices both conditionally inversely.

The study presents a detailed examination of shock-compressed alkali metals (Li, Na, K, and Rb) utilizing extensive experimental datasets and key theoretical advancements. First, a new equation of state (EOS) was developed and applied to shock compression; this model adheres to the corresponding states principle and is valid for simple metals under conditions of high density and pressure (where density exceeds the zero-pressure value by more than 10% and pressure surpasses 1 GPa). Second, the analysis incorporated the impact of ionization on the EOS, drawing on recent theoretical insights. Finally, the partial ionization degree was calculated for shocked alkali metals across the specific EOS regions, with findings showing strong agreement across experimental results and theoretical frameworks.

The study investigates the thermal equilibrium dynamics of heavy vector mesons embedded within a parity-violating environment that includes both the Born-Infinfield mass term and the Chern-Simons (CS) term. This work builds on the formalism developed by Creutz and colleagues in 1985, which describes massive electroweak sphaleron transitions using the gauge field configuration space where the winding number changes by an integer amount (the winding number is defined as the topological charge of the gauge field). By exploring the relationship between the winding number and the action associated with each configuration, the authors have derived the partition function for this system. Furthermore, they compute the rate of change of the winding number as a function of the external magnetic field, finding that it decreases monotonically as the winding number increases. They also demonstrate how the induced electric current, which causes a non-Abelian anomaly in this context, leads to changes in charge conjugation of the winding number, which they show is proportional to the winding number itself.

This paper introduces a randomized distributed algorithm designed to estimate the volume of distributed networks. The proposed model uses a constant-time algorithm that converges with high probability and has near optimal variance per node in terms of volume estimation errors. The variance also has a very low upper bound that the proof demonstrates to be tight using the worst-case example network structure for estimation errors. The paper further shows a connection between the volume problem in distributed networks and a well established problem known as the network centrality problem. The center network nodes problem asks to find the probability distribution over all nodes where the distance to the center is the key metric for probability. The proposed center network nodes problem allows us to show a strong link between the two types of problems. Finally, the paper shows that the proposed center network nodes problem provides the variance upper bound for estimation errors.

The LAZIX project investigates whether large liquid xenon detectors can effectively manage the extensive photon and electron loads required for the highly precise neutrino inversion signature sought by JUNO. Comprising four individually scalable, 1-meter class test modules—each measuring 1 m³—their spatial arrangement replicates a scaled-back version of JUNO's final detector geometry, including its position-dependent density distribution of 1,3-di-2-propyl-ovalcine. Illuminated by an array of 300 blue 436-nm LEDs, our results indicate that even under these intense light conditions, our small-scale prototypes, which feature 300 simulated JUNO-style MPW sensors and 300 simulated GB2055-photopmultiplier per cubic meter, can process the resulting photoelectron and signal density.

This paper introduces an enhanced Informer architecture designed for Multidimensional Multivary Time Series Prediction (TMTP). While the original Informer model excels at capturing long-term dependencies within unidimensional sequences, it is limited regarding the inter-relationship analysis between distinct dimensions. To overcome this, the proposed model embeds cross-attention modules to explicitly model interactions among dimensions and integrates three specific modules—self-attention, mutual-attention, and cross-attention—to produce three corresponding sequence of attention maps. These maps provide valuable insights by revealing the relationships among time steps, variable dimensions, and the input feature data. Extensive experiments on diverse real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed model surpasses state-of-the-art alternatives in predictive accuracy. Furthermore, the generated attention maps validate the model's efficacy in modeling sequential dependencies and cross-dimensional interactions.

In supervised learning, models are trained to perform specific tasks using labeled examples. However, including label associations during the inference phase often leads to suboptimal outcomes compared to a label-free approach. To address this, we propose PILE (Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble), a framework that utilizes labels only in the form of pairwise comparisons during inference to enhance model predictions. The core mechanism of PILE involves iteratively refining the final output scores by leveraging relative label information to resolve ambiguious cases. We evaluate the method across various data scarcity scenarios, specifically on classification tasks with few training instances classified by natural language. Despite the small quantity of training available, the system demonstrates a robust capability to accurately classify based on natural text descriptions provided. Specifically when a textual description accompanies each image within comparable image sets, a marked improvement occurs in accuracy rates when allowing the use of textual information during the inference stage itself. When assessing standard or average classification performance metrics across multiple experimental setups, there exists an eight-point relative increase over baseline methods that ignore textual comparisons entirely.

This approach significantly enhances the signal-to-noise ratio within the combined output compared to isolated devices, effectively extending the potential reach for detecting dark matter signals to larger masses of the ultralight bosons.

The field of programmable network switches has grown significantly over the last few years, driven primarily by the P4 language, which offers hardware-independent capabilities. These advances have fueled a surge in related academic studies. However, the field struggles with a lack of transparent, open-source P4 compiler backends for various programmable switches, rendering many existing programs difficult to verify and analyze. To address this, we present a transparent and verifiable P4 backend implemented on Ryuzi, a controllable software switch. Our solution features a P4-to-Ryozu frontend that parses instructions, identifies control flow, and performs analysis, alongside a custom P4 semantic model to clarify instruction meanings. Additionally, we have developed a P4 type system that narrows the gap between theoretical static definitions and practical implementations. Testing via the switch emulation emulator on various functional programs—including established and new programs—demonstrates that this approach effectively enables both functional verification and structural analysis.

Under specific conditions, this modified approach yields exact and known solutions, achieving higher precision than standard methods. Further, a new efficient and straightforward strategy is introduced to handle scenarios where $b$ exhibits complexity, demonstrating that the proposed technique offers superior performance relative to existing standard techniques.

Chaotic scattering occurs within time-dependent dynamical systems where an orbit eventually exits a bounded region of phase space, and the prediction of its escape time becomes area-invariant of initial condition resolution due to conditionality instability. In the context of non-overlapping disks moving periodically, three-body non-intersecting Wada basins can be constructed, all of which are stable even under arbitrarily small damping conditions. The present analysis extends the examination of these systems to include weak dissipation, which alters the structural stability of Wada basins: Wada configurations stable without dissipation now lose this stability once any amount of dissipation is introduced. The escape times for trajectories are analyzed as functions of initial conditions, and the conditionality and spatial limits of predictability are determined. It is observed that for a given level of dissipation, the baseline predictability limit remains roughly constant across most of the phase space, but it degrades significantly within a specific zone adjacent to Wada points outside the basin boundaries. This dissipation-induced effect also manifests as a dramatic contraction of the domain containing points with infinite predictability, which were previously unlimited. Furthermore, the count of regions where predictability is infinite declines from three bodies (which lacks dissipation) to two. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that for any two periodic orbits, the separation in escape-time predictability grows logarithmically with respect to their initial separation as dissipation weakens, approaching infinity only in the limit of zero damping.

We introduce a low-energy effective field theory within the framework of composite Higgs models, specifically utilizing partial striction of the strong custodial symmetry to yield a five-parameter scenario. This setup allows for interaction with the muon g-2 anomaly, potential searches at a muon collider, and investigation capabilities at low-energy hadron colliders such as the TeV-scale colliders. Our study proposes an extensive scan of the five-dimensional parameter space, testing the model's compatibility with existing constraints while addressing the g-2 muon discrepancy and future collider prospects.

Human Video Understanding (HVA) addresses the challenge of modeling interactions among objects and scenes within video content. This paper introduces HON, a novel deep learning framework that integrates the hierarchical attention structure with the temporal focus of HHN to explicitly capture temporal distinctions and spatial relationships across frames. Specifically, the network's multiple spatial-temporal attention (STTM) mechanism identifies critical areas and temporal shifts in continuous video data, while also being guided by a hierarchical attention layer to concentrate signal on significant regions across different video scales. To further refine this process, HON employs a hierarchical attention-based STTM to filter out dominant and critical details, ensuring only significant information proceeds through subsequent processing. By modulating temporal transitions and spatial priorities effectively, HON enhances its capacity for comprehensive video interpretation. HON achieved superior performance on two public datasets, the U4 and Action, where it established new state-of-the-art benchmarks in understanding complex video actions and events.

This investigation examines how scattering of scalar fields affects the fate of black hole remnants that possess either a charge slightly less than their extremal threshold ($|\extremality| < 1$) or are already fully extremal. We find that the outcome depends entirely on the scattering's intensity. At low intensities, the remnant settles into a standard black hole state; however, at high intensities, its final configuration evolves into an exotic object—a "eclectic black hole"—characterized by a negative, yet finite, mass. Specifically, we analyze two distinct scenarios: first, a multi-particle scattering event occurring at the remnant's surface, and second, an effective slow-roll of the remnant through spacetime due to high-energy scattering. Analysis reveals a paradox where an object with negative mass becomes stable even against variations in scale (a hallmark feature distinguishing these objects from our previous findings on near-extremal remnant collapse). Consequently, these eclectic black holes are not merely a result of a different collapse mechanism but represent a fundamentally distinct type of object.

Star formation is a fundamental cosmic process linked to the origins of planetary systems and potentially the universe itself. As such, scientists study it extensively to unravel the mysteries of the solar system's creation and life on Earth; we currently possess a comprehensive understanding of the physical and chemical mechanisms driving it. We have extensively explored the morphological and statistical changes associated with stars as they form, relying on both a vast array of observations and sophisticated numerical simulations. Despite these efforts, the formal definition of the star formation rate (SFR) remains elusive because its measurement involves complex observational and numerical complexities, including variations in mass resolution, cloud models, and numerical schemes. We propose a new formalism for calculating the SFR that offers high fidelity while maintaining simplicity. We define the SFR as the statistical expectation of the newly formed mass per unit time and volume, utilizing smoothed-particle hydrodynamics (SPH) to model self-gravitating stars. This formal design is adaptable to various simulation types, from global boxes to local regions. When applied to global simulations, the formalism yields a result aligned with conventional SFR measurement techniques. However, its true power emerges in high-resolution local cloud simulations, where it provides the SFR with superior accuracy, making it particularly suitable for large ensembles of cloud formation simulations.

Symbolic computation of entropy is essential for the inference of models based on data, but this process is challenging when the probability distributions cannot be directly evaluated. This study presents a strategy to calculate and compare relative entropy between two symbolic discrete distributions, $p(x)$ and $q(x)$, by leveraging their joint properties. Our method relies on expressing relative entropy via power matching (or power alignment) indices of $p$ and $q$. These power indices are demonstrated to be linked to the moments of synthetic random variables. Consequently, we can establish inequalities bounding the relative entropy between $p$ and $q$ by approximating the moments of such auxiliary variables. The approach is validated through several examples, including its application in modeling and comparing power-law distributions.

Network Traffic Analysis (NTA) employs various techniques to detect both established and emerging threats by analyzing the protocol layers of network traffic. While these methods are highly effective for data-rich servers and cloud environments, they struggle on limited-resource devices such as cell phones and tablets due to the computational and memory constraints that prevent the use of complex models like convolutional or recurrent neural networks. Although limited-resource units can safely host basic detectors for high-risk, well-known threats, emerging threats often require attack identification models that exceed their local processing capacity in the cloud. Cloud deployment presents its own issues, specifically the high latency inherent in roundtrips between devices and servers. To resolve the combined challenges of on-device and cloud-based limitations in resource-constrained scenarios, this study proposes NBcoded, a tool that offloads computationally burdensome processes to local computing units within the same data center. This approach is designed to significantly lower latency compared to traditional cloud solutions.

Subgroups of index $p$ in a group $G$, where $p$ is a prime, form a subgroup itself in the context of finite group theory. The growth difference between two subgroups in a group is a key indicator of the group's structural properties, such as being finitely presented or torsion-free.

Video recordings offer valuable insights into various biological processes by capturing the movement of entities. However, a significant challenge remains in distinguishing pathological from healthy biological motion within this data. Since biological and non-biological objects often appear similar in visual recordings, conventional object detection methods are often insufficient for characterizing specific biological movement. To address this, we introduce **Biomotion**, an new framework that analyzes video content to capture the dynamics of biological entities. Unlike existing approaches, Biomotion first identifies potential biological entities and subsequently characterizes their motion using a **Markov Switching System**. This allows for the quantification of travel speed and the probability of direction changes. Validated through extensive testing on three distinct datasets, our characterization proves highly robust for a wide range of biological scenarios. Notably, when applied to medical datasets, the framework yields specific metrics that enable the discrimination of pathological entities from healthy ones.

Nonadiabatic Born effective charges in insulators are predicted to be similar in all directions with values close to unity, whereas in clean conductors they are expected to be directionally dependent and large. We introduce a method to compute these charges for materials containing disordered vacancies; unlike the ideal scenarios above, our findings for insulators with defects show vector-like behavior and magnitudes that can far exceed unit one. Furthermore, in disordered conductors, these charges maintain directionality and high magnitudes that are stable and uniform over a broad range of temperature conditions. The magnitude of the nonadiabatic Born charge is directly proportional to the degree of disorder present in the material. In both cleaner insulators and materials with milder disorganization, phonon interactions cause a significant reduction in both charge magnitude and material-specific anisotropy. Ultimately, the computed directional properties of these charges offer new strategies for generating strongly pyroelectric effects specifically within defective materials.

We analyze a fluid governed by the fluctuating hydrodynamics equation, which extends the deterministic Navier-Stokes equation by including a multiplicative noise term. Through numerical simulations, we assess the equation's capacity to reproduce turbulence dissipation and the observed "four-thirds law" for energy flux at the inertial range's boundary. The results indicate that fluctuating hydrodynamics effectively captures the essential features of deterministic turbulence regarding energy dissipation and the four-thirds law, although compliance with the law exhibits significant spatial and temporal variability. In contrast, energy production driven by the noise is confined to the viscous sublayer and the inertial range while remaining negligible elsewhere this contradicts findings from prior studies suggesting that fluctuating hydrodynamics could explain anomalous dissipation in deterministic turbulence by providing a physical mechanism for it. Our data shows that the statistical properties of energy flux and production share similarities, yet the magnitudes of these quantities arise from fundamentally different mechanisms. The predominant source of fluctuation in energy dissipation is the inertial range, whereas the dominant source of energy production is the viscous sublayer, thereby explaining why the deterministic and stochastic contributions to the four-thirds law are distributed across the domain, with the resulting fluctuations in the viscous domain being of a lower order of magnitude.

Solids that exhibit reverse magnetoelectric coupling can transform into a state where applying a magnetic field induces electric polarization, a phenomenon known as the Witten effect. This study investigates the role of "softness"—the ease with which a crystal's atomic structure can be distorted—on the emergence of this effect. It is observed that both the magnitude of the induced polarization and its reliance on external field orientation are significantly influenced by this structural flexibility. Conversely, the effect's reliance on field strength appears largely independent of softness. However, the existence of zero-field metastable polar states, a signature of switched polarity, remains mostly unaffected by structural modifications. This result suggests that while traditional routes of countermeasuring might struggle to consistently eliminate these hidden states, targeting specific materials with optimized softness levels offers a viable strategy for minimizing them. These findings are demonstrated across cubic perovskites like BaTiO$_3$, as well as their engineered "swapped" counterparts, PbTiZrO, and "inverse" variants, Ba(ZrO), demonstrating the practical relevance of the theory.

This study introduces two novel design-mining techniques to resolve the issues of fragile conclusions and limited relevance across different datasets. Correlation analysis of light curves from spatially separated quasars offers a pathway to testing theories of cosmic geometry and gravity. This study explores how incorporating the measured correlation lag into the analysis can enhance observational outcomes. Specifically, the correlation lag serves to bolster statistical power and can be utilized to optimize observational strategies. To achieve this, we introduce a novel variable for analyzing time-varying sources, which we name "the correlation times," and we examine its properties. Using this framework, the correlation lag can be integrated directly into the standard least-squares fitting process. Furthermore, the correlation times provide a method for estimating an optimal strategy for both future and retrospective (retrospective) observations of a specific object, thereby determining the most efficient timing and duration between observations. When applied to current or planned surveys, this new variable and associated observation method yield significantly higher statistical power than traditional techniques, which do not utilize correlation lags. Additionally, these capabilities allow the correlation times to serve as precise tools for observing correlations across supermassive black holes.

Relational models offer enhanced capabilities compared to standard models, which have been significantly advancing the field of pharmacology. With connections spanning from chemistry to clinical trials and connections, the information cannot be fully represented in a structured manner, which is necessary for effective pharmacological analysis and development of new drugs. This paper introduces a novel method for road condition monitoring that leverages the widespread smartphone usage across diverse nations. By capturing image data from these devices, the proposed system allows for the real-time assessment of road status, with the distinct advantage that infrastructure can be directed to address only the problematic areas identified. The study presents a machine learning framework that utilizes public mobility dataset images to train the model, removing the need to gather physical images from the target regions; this method is particularly effective when GPR data are unavailable. The approach is designed to be easily deployable in new countries within hours, offering significant potential for widespread adoption and the improvement of existing road management methodologies.

Imitation learning is a highly effective approach for acquiring new skills by having an observer analyze demonstrated actions. A major hurdle, however, remains when there is a gap between the environment in which an agent performs its tasks and the environment used to generate the training data; even slight discrepancies can cause standard methods to fail completely. This paper introduces a domain randomization strategy aimed at bridging this environmental divide. By employing a two-phase training process, an implicit mapping is learned to translate observed actions into appropriate responses for varying contexts. Experimental results confirm that this technique successfully enables sophisticated behaviors, allowing simple agents to mimic skillful performance even when both the source and target environments differ significantly.

Protostar formation involves the gravitational collapse of a rotating gas cloud, during which angular momentum conservation causes the formation of a rotating accretion disk. While the classical angular-vortex model links angular velocity to collapse time—predicting that high angular momentum leads to longer collapse times—a new model suggests angular momentum may instead trigger disk fragmentation during protostar birth. This new framework incorporates turbulent viscosity and argues that angular momentum accumulation shortens collapse duration by reducing it. The model evaluates whether disks form and fragment under a wide range of initial angular momentum distributions, indicating that disk formation is likely across most collapsing clouds and that disk fragmentation occurs in regions of low density and high temperature. These findings suggest that a significant fraction of young stars are born from fragmented disks and are therefore expected to exhibit multiple mass distributions at early stages, with only a small fraction of young stars having formed from non-fragmented disks.

Association rules constitute fundamental knowledge about attribute relationships derived from rule sets exhibiting various forms of redundancy. While algorithmic methods exist to eliminate these forms, they lack visibility into redundant forms' nature. This paper addresses such redundancy in terms of logical entailment and characterizes it using the concept of rule sets' independence. Additionally, we characterize these forms of redundancy through concepts of models and defined a property concerning sets of entailment. These concepts were utilized to design specific, novel, straightforward, and effective algorithms for identifying associated redundancy in rules. Finally, our findings regarding independence and entailment serve as a basis for further analysis, including defining the number of association rules as NP-complete problems.

This study investigates whether geographic variations in mental health treatment and access to such services influence recidivism rates among offenders who underwent a mandatory psychological evaluation. We utilize treatment availability in the county where an offender committed their crime as a proxy for access to services. Using data on over 10,000 inmates from Pennsylvania spanning 1999 to 2009, our analyses—both aggregated and detailed by crime type—examine the link between treatment availability and recidivism. We find that increased mental health treatment access significantly lowers the probability of reoffending, particularly for those involving drug-related and violent acts. These reductions in recidivism are partially driven by improved psychological functioning, specifically better impulse control and reduced aggression.

This paper establishes the orthogonality relations for Genie's polynomial, using them as a foundation to examine their properties through generating functions. The study of these relations serves to illuminate the behavior of Genie's polynomial, with the purpose of providing a comprehensive analysis.

Radio source maps are vital for the future of astronomy, yet their high dimensionality and sparse data from radio telescopes complicate the inversion process. This study introduces a novel approach where a map uncertainty metric guides the optimization of a virtual sensor strategy for data acquisition. By employing an adaptive sampling process, the proposal seeks to optimize where observations are virtually made, thereby enhancing radio source map reconstruction.

Deep learning models are capable of identifying data patterns; however, issues like concept drift and the resulting emergence of anomalies often go unchecked without labeled training data for supervision. This research introduces the use of unsupervised learning models to detect anomalies, eliminating the necessity for labeled data through three approaches: monitoring prediction confidence levels, analyzing predicted distribution density for to spot outliers, or comparing new inputs against established patterns using distance metrics. The paper reviews existing unsupervised methods for anomaly detection and introduces the concept of integrated drift detection via an innovative synthesis of several techniques, the LDMDD. This new model leverages multiple detection strategies to identify drift more reliably in the presence of noisy inputs and sparse datasets. The proposed LDMDD framework was tested and compared against leading supervised, online, and traditional methods using the U4AnD benchmark for its ability to identify drift in diverse contexts. The results indicate that the LDMDD model outperforms the other methods.

Human speech is frequently captured in noisy environments, rendering the signals unreliable for the accurate verification of user identities. Advanced digital systems are intended to supplement or replace these imperfect inputs by processing audio under adverse conditions; however, the performance of these systems often degrades when faced with such noise. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel fuzzy logic based noise estimator. Experimental results indicate that this proposed model achieves peak accuracy of 95.85% in clean acoustic environments and a success rate of 90.10% within noisy conditions, demonstrating robust efficacy across all tested scenarios.

Data augmentation is a well-established technique for enhancing the performance of computer-aided diagnosis systems. In clinical contexts, it is often employed to overcome limited training data by artificially expanding datasets. This study examines how different strategies affect performance: does it yield greater benefits when applied to small or large datasets, and can it consistently enhance system reliability? We addressed these questions by evaluating multiple augmentation techniques against a, and a, classification task using the Microsoft Research Conversation State Actuation dataset. Experiments revealed that data augmentation successfully improves performance on both large and small datasets while maintaining original model robustness; however, it produces superior gains when data is scarce. Furthermore, we introduced a new robustness metric to assess model stability and a novel method for identifying non-informative augmentations. These insights enable more reliable deployment of augmentation strategies in practical applications. The authors' robustness check reveals that models trained with data augmentation on large training sets often exhibit similar robustness to those trained without it, whereas training on small datasets may yield non-robust models. Given this, data augmentation should be applied with caution using small batches and careful parameter tuning. Additionally, we proposed a, and a, dataset to explore the effects of data augmentation in a, and a, providing a foundation for future research.

This conceptual framework, defined on the sample level and constructed from a perspective parallel to $L_p$ spaces, provides another setting for the ergodic theory. We demonstrate that any ergodic $\phi$-complete $q$-Langley $\eta$-space admits a sequence of weak complete convergent probability measures to a $q$-Langley $\eta$-space with a stochastic parameter. Estimators and their consistency under this convergence type are discussed, with asymptotical normal distribution of the $q$-Langley $\eta$-space parameter estimator being proven. Furthermore, central limit theorems for sums of random variables defined by $q$-Langley $\eta$-space are established, with direct consequences for the hypothesis test of the $q$-Langley $\eta$-space population location being derived.

Engineering and science across the global spectrum are increasingly adopting high-throughput, time-tagged data analysis to manage the vast volumes of digital information produced by modern detectors and sensors. Conventional processing systems, however, are often constrained by the limited parallelization of legacy software, in addition to the inherent computational barriers of data volume and memory limitations. To overcome these obstacles, we have developed the Extensible Time-tagged Analyzer (ETA), a Python-based framework designed for scalable and flexible data management capable of performing sophisticated, multi-stage transformations. Designed with a pipeline-oriented workflow architecture, ETA facilitates both rapid prototyping and the creation of highly specialized, optimized pipelines through an array of modular tools and data formats. Validated through demonstrations of several pivotal projects within the International Linear Collider community, these applications highlight the platform's capacity to resolve limiting factors found in historical analysis infrastructures.

We present an existence and a solution theorem for mean field game models with general regular conditions, indicating that equilibrium availability is often compromised by strict smoothness mandates. To address this, we utilize the concept of regular equilibria, which permits discontinuities within the open domain of the game while enforcing specific selection criteria on the solution choices within such zero-measure sets. In scenarios where smoothness conditions are met, the proposed approach yields a proof of an alternative nature that is both quantitative and qualitative, relying on the selection method previously developed in [Cascetta, 2020]. This technique selects solutions from the set of Nash equilibria based on specific criteria, including one that ensures the utility function for the mean field of best responses remains as regular as possible, including in cases where it is not differentiable.

A key goal in the search by the Gaia mission is the identification of present-day stellar strings resulting from the cosmic inflation. To enable this search, a method grounded in the concept of "common proper motion" has been developed specifically to define and identify these strings within the Gaia dataset. Applying this algorithm to a simulated Gaia data set created by the Eniaia simulation, the analysis examined the derived strings for signs of internal chemical inhomogeneity. A measurement using the Gaia GR19 index demonstrated that a present-day string formed in the early universe would exhibit a dispersion in Gaia GR19 values roughly an order of magnitude smaller than the dispersion of local field stars, indicating that a typical string is about a factor of 100 to a factor of 1000 times more chemically uniform.

Recent advancements in generative technology allow users to easily create digital and physical fashion items, leading to a surge in user-generated content across social media and collaboration platforms where users design unique apparel. However, this proliferation has introduced challenges, notably the manual identification of aesthetic inconsistencies in assembled outfits. In this study, we introduce a deep learning framework designed to detect specific mismatched items within custom outfits constructed by users. This system is highly relevant to applications like automated recommendation engines and collaboration tools where teams tailor apparel collectively. By inputting images of each individual item, the proposed method discerns fine-grained details to pinpoint any incompatible pieces. We have established the Benchmark of Custom Outfits (BCO) dataset, which contains 38,000+ images of complete custom outfits created by numerous individuals, annotated specifically to support the training and evaluation of algorithms designed for item mismatch detection.

Nonclassical resource theories are expanding the landscape of quantum information theories. While resource theories have emerged as a pivotal framework for unifying and generalizing concepts within quantum theories, their adaptation to scenarios where actions or states lack "classicality"—rendering standard tools like probability distributions and expectation values inadequate—remains a significant and challenging hurdle. This paper explores the application of operator geometric mean as a unifying method across multiple such theories, covering resources like asymmetry, entropy, and compatibility, thereby offering a fresh perspective on geometric quantum states and measurements, and proving the existence of generally joint measurements for effects within these resources.

Federated Learning (FL) stands out as a privacy-focused machine learning framework that guarantees the absence of client data during model training. Although early FL was designed primarily for edge devices like smartphones and tablets—which have constrained computing power, it scaled poorly for high-performance networks. The evolution toward federated buffer algorithms has offered a solution by dividing training into two distinct phases to boost scalability. This paper introduces Buffert, an enhanced buffer algorithm that preserves privacy through the Generalized Puffer concept by ensuring proportional aggregation for fair contributions by all clients to global updates during federated buffer training by optimizing resource allocation via client selection based on historical performance metrics and connecting them over a public or internal network architecture designed to support high-speed communication requirements at scale and offering improved balance between efficiency and security in machine learning applications.

This paper introduces and examines the commutant $\Gamma$ of polynomial shift semigroups on the Fock space. The authors demonstrate that any operator $T$ belonging to $\Gamma$ can expressed in a derived calculus form, showing that the calculus's image covers the entire commutant. Furthermore, a sufficient condition is provided for a calculus operator to be normal. The study derives its spectrum and spectral type with explicit determination, using these properties to establish a spectral analysis, and the distinction between the calculus and an abstract commutant is explored.

Although the traditional Hawking radiation model suggests that primordial black holes (PBHs) across all masses cannot constitute the entirety of dark matter due to severe overlimits on PBH abundance imposed by radiation constraints, we identify conditions where they can, specifically when the PBH population is segmented into multiple distinct clusters in parameter space where formation is uncorrelated between clusters. By employing Monte Carlo simulations to simulate the formation of such clustered PBH clusters, we demonstrate that the five most recently identified dark matter candidates—all parameter sets implying a total dark matter composition exclusively of PBHs—actually represent five separate clusters. Crucially, while individual formation processes are overconstrained by existing constraints, the largest clusters within each group remain under the limits required to aggregate into the correct dark matter density. In every one these cases analyzed, PBHs with masses roughly between $10^{-10}$ and $10^{-7}$ solar masses emerge as the dominant component. Consequently, PBHs in this specific mass window are permitted to form in sufficiently high abundances to significantly impact the interpretation of dark matter across all relevant theoretical frameworks regarding the over/under-abundancy issue.

This work models a dry-cracking-like fault network arising from particle raft disassembly in a particle-bath system. As a gel-like particle gel detaches from the glass substrate and expands, a fluid-filled particle raft forms a shell around the aggregate; upon deflation, a raft sheds off, leaving behind a network of particle-rich structures that resemble earthquake faults. This dry-cracking phenomenon is driven by a balance between two competing forces: particle re-aggregation and the gel's expansion. A dimensionless parameter is defined as the ratio of particle diffusion to raft expansion, which is used to compare the gel's expansion rate to particle diffusion. This model is validated by calculating the distance between adjacent rifts and comparing it to the theoretical spacing predicted by dry-cracking. Experiments show that increasing the expansion speed results in a longer distance between rifs, which aligns with predictions.

Gallium nitride (GaN) remains a primary choice for high-power and high-frequency applications thanks to its robust theoretical potential; however, lattice-matching growth on silicon is essential for achieving large-scale production and lower costs. The rapid expansion of COVID-19 necessitates the implementation of timely intervention policies to slow transmission. While medical effectiveness are in conflict, timely intervention policies are required to contain spread. However, such measures come with economic costs. Thus, pandemic containment requires balancing infection control with economic costs. We propose a novel approach combining deep reinforcement learning and a speed limit model to optimize this trade-off by recommending the best policy string based on the pandemic's current stage. Additionally, we develop a simulation framework using actual data from China and Japan to evaluate policy impacts on infection rates and recoveries while measuring associated economic impacts. We demonstrate that adaptive, state-based strategies significantly reduce the speed and volume of infections relative to constant strict or lenient policies without significantly increasing economic losses.

This paper introduces DataScope, a visualization framework designed to streamline debugging of machine learning pipelines against data inconsistencies. Currently, ML engineering relies heavily on manual inspection and ad-hoc scripts to identify such issues, a process that is both tedious and inefficient. To overcome these limitations, we present DataScope, which offers coherent support for profiling, searching, and transforming datasets across a broad range of structures. Specifically, the scope supports relational data, graph-based networks, and document-oriented formats like JSON. By integrating transformation logic with visual interaction and providing features to isolate subsets tied to specific invariants, DataScope significantly accelerates the identification of problems. Comprehensive case studies reveal that the framework effectively assists practitioners in finding mistakes faster and yields novel discoveries regarding data quality. The system is implemented in web-based interface at [DataScope](https://datascope.i2.ac.ugto.mx/).

Mn$_3$N3n is recognized as a topological half-metallic ferromagnet, yet its experimentally observed stable ferromagnetic ground state contradicts predictions from first-principles calculations that show no magnetic order in this material. To resolve this discrepancy, this study incorporates the trimerization effect observed in the experimental structure during magnetic ordering within the simulations. Including trimerization reveals that the pure nonmagnetic state becomes less stable than a states where Mn atoms possess identical, robust magnetic moments of 3.85$\mu_B$. Although prior Monte Carlo simulations using standard Heisenberg models failed to reproduce the experimental Curie temperature (Tc) under this assumption, introducing effective antiferromagnetic exchange interactions of approximately 30 meV between neighboring trimers successfully achieves the experimental Tc. Additionally, analyzing the density of states shows that this effective interaction stems from ferromagnetic coupling within each triangle and dominant antiferromagnetic inter-triangle coupling. Finally, we calculate the topological Hall effect, finding it arises from magnetic domains with out-of-plane magnetization that carry non-trivial topologies such as conical and skyrmion structures.

We present an approach to Relation Extraction that leverages Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) for the fine-grained prediction of relation boundaries. To achieve this, we have developed a novel architecture known as DRNN (Dual Recurrent Neural Network), which employs two interconnected DNNs to precisely locate the start and end positions of constituents within relational phrases. This dual-network mechanism enables our model to generate full-span predictions for constituents, such as relation head and tail, independently of one another. Furthermore, our framework facilitates the shared learning of relation-specific patterns and head/tail compositions across different contexts. Experimental results on four established benchmarks demonstrate that our proposed DRNN model significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art baselines.

Recreating hypergraphs from their projections is a critical challenge in analyzing graph-derived datasets. Previous efforts focused on treating reconstruction as an optimization problem to find the ideal hypergraph, relying on algorithms sensitive to initial conditions in the process. This work introduces a different strategy utilizing the properties of set partitions. Specifically, we present conditions determining when a projected set system can exactly represent a given hypergraph and offer an algorithm to simplify these overrepresented set partitions, resulting in smoother projections.

This paper introduces PAXRay, a novel dataset comprising 3,333 image-ray pairs paired with radiological observations. Each image is accompanied by 1 to 5 three-dimensional bounding boxes representing the objects or regions depicted in the text. Our primary goal is to leverage this data for teaching vision-language models to construct three-dimensional visual grounding in radiology. Currently, no public datasets offer bounding boxes for radiological descriptions, rendering available data for text-to-3D radiology interpretation scarce. Furthermore, existing public 3D bounding box datasets, such as COCO, often include annotations for medical content irrelevant to radiological reports. Consequently, pre-training on COCO could bias radiology-specific models toward general objects and regions rather than radiological observations. Our proposal involves adapting pre-trained models using Ray texts annotated with 3D boxes to enhance their relevance to radiological content, rather than creating models from scratch. Our findings demonstrate that PAXRay yields superior performance on the COCO medical sub-task and enables models to converge more rapidly during fine-tuning compared to approaches using ray texts devoid of spatial information or those lacking spatial annotations.

We introduce MaNav, a single, unified multi-modal policy designed for robot navigation. MaNav integrates visual data from one or more cameras, including camera poses, and is trained using a reinforcement learning approach to optimize a mutual information objective. Specifically, the visual encoder is updated to encode future states relative to the agent's current state and action, while the navigation policy is trained to maximize the information the resulting action sequences convey about the modal observations. This design establishes a tight coupling between the policy and the encoder, allowing the agent to discover an effective strategy for a specific perception capability or, conversely, to optimize its capabilities under specific strategic constraints. We evaluate MaNav in diverse, randomly generated environments across several benchmarks, demonstrating that it consistently outperforms prior methods. Notably, MaNav achieves a remarkable 300% improvement in tasks requiring the exploration of novel domains.

This study examines the cosmological distribution of merger events for white dwarf binaries derived from Population III stars, which are the heaviest remnant objects from the first generation of stellar collapses. Such systems serve as potential progenitors for Mergers of massive objects (MOBs). Our models incorporate intricate physics, including complex stellar evolution and the subsequent dynamical formation of these double-degenerate systems. We find that the cosmic distribution of these mergers peaks around $z \sim 1.5$, corresponding to an estimated event rate of $\sim 10^{-10}$ year$^{-1}$ Gpc$^{-3}$ at that redshift. However, when integrated to cosmological volumes relevant for observational surveys (such as $\sim 10^{-10}$ year$^{-1}$ Gpc$^{-3}$), these Population III systems account for only a small fraction of MOBs because the total event density is orders of magnitude lower than that of shorter-period systems ($\sim 10^{-10}$ year$^{-1}$ Gpc$^{-3}$) with long merger timescales.

This research examines a data-driven approach to identifying incidents in storage-equipped grid systems. We develop methods that enable planners and operators to detect, isolate, and reconfigure issues within energy storage units and their surrounding grids, even in the absence of direct measurements from the distribution network. Following detection, we apply a scheme using power flow analysis to determine the precise location of incidents. We validate our methods using a detailed electromagnetic simulator with simulated data drawn from a representative storage installation, verifying the algorithm's effectiveness in a context where distribution-level telemetry is unavailable. We further demonstrate how the approach scales to scenarios lacking analytical power flow models.

Robot control algorithms frequently rely on the concept of a manipulability matrix or ellipsoid associated with each rigid body. Typical definitions either link them directly to specific Riemannian manifolds on that body or characterize them as distinct Riemandan structures, such as ellipsoids within a Riemandan manifold of ellipsoids. This paper clarifies potential misconceptions regarding such objects by constructing a manifold of manipulability ellipses and examining its properties. The authors prove that when defined in this way, the manipulability ellipses form a manifold that is not sectionable by a Riemandan structure and does not support a gradient flow; consequently, a Riemandan manifold structure must be assumed for mathematical consistency if analyzing properties through a manifold approach.

This study introduces a tagger based signal utilizing a technique with the Initial State Radiation (ISR) jet in top quark pair ($t\bar{t}$) events for the Higgs boson ($H$) search within the $H \rightarrow b\bar{b}$ decay mode. By exploiting the substantial invariant mass difference between the Higgs and the $b\bar{ t}$ system, the resulting $t\bar t$ system's transverse momentum ($p_T$) serves as a powerful discriminator to separate signal from background. Monte Carlo simulations indicate an expected signal-to-background ratio of approximately 1 in the selected $t\bar t-\to 2~jet$+X($p^2_{Tp}$) > 1000 GeV$^2$ region for the $H \rightarrow b\bar t$ channel at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s} = 14$ TeV and an integrated luminosity of 300 fb$^{-1}$. This approach is expected to achieve a signal-to-background ratio of about 1 in $H \rightarrow b\bar t$ events with a center-of-mass energy of 14 TeV and a dataset size exceeding 300 fb$^{-1}$. This work provides the first investigation of the feasibility of the jet $H \rightarrow t\bar t$-associated production in $t\bar t$ decays.

We demonstrate during an initial unsupervised phase using randomly rotated poses and apply pose-labels in subsequent stages to achieve higher accuracy. We evaluate this approach on multiple 3D tasks, including object detection and pose estimation, without relying on 3D cues during training; our results with CUB dataset 3Ds show improved performance on canonical pose learning, matching or surpassing existing methods that utilize 3D data.
